WIDER CONTEXT
- The City of New York stopped accepting ABC No Rio's rent checks in 1994 and began eviction proceedings against it at 156 Rivington Street, where Asian Americans for Equality planned to convert the four-storey tenement into affordable housing (The New York Times, Andrew Jacobs, "Arts Group Wins Eviction Battle", 23 February 1997).
- After a sit-in at the headquarters of the Department of Housing Preservation and Development on 5 February 1997, outgoing commissioner Liliam Barrios-Paoli agreed to drop the eviction proceedings, on condition that the group raise at least $100,000 for renovation and that about six squatters leave the building. Board president Dave Powell said "resistence pays" (The New York Times).
- ABC No Rio's own history states that more than 2,500 people signed petitions against the eviction and that five supporters were arrested in New York in February 1997 while demonstrating (ABC No Rio).

- In 2020 the Paul Rudolph Foundation sued the Paul Rudolph Institute for Modern Architecture (PRIMA, formerly the Paul Rudolph Heritage Foundation) and Ernst Wagner, Rudolph's executor and residuary beneficiary, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Part of the case concerned the ownership and copyright status of works by Paul Rudolph or his office (Paul Rudolph Institute for Modern Architecture, press release, 21 July 2023).
- On 8 September 2022 the court ruled that the Paul Rudolph works in the Paul Rudolph Collection at the Library of Congress are in the public domain, and noted that Wagner may hold rights to material outside that collection, according to the Institute's release, which cites The Paul Rudolph Foundation, Inc. v. Paul Rudolph Heritage Foundation et al., 2022 WL 4109723 (S.D.N.Y. Sep. 8, 2022).
- The parties settled all claims in July 2023 on confidential terms (Paul Rudolph Institute for Modern Architecture).

SOURCES
- https://www.paulrudolph.institute/s/20230721-Settlement-Press-Release.pdf

ID: institute-of-contemporary-art-philadelphia-ica

WIDER CONTEXT
- In December 1988 "Robert Mapplethorpe: The Perfect Moment" opened at the Institute of Contemporary Art, which received a $30,000 grant from the National Endowment for the Arts for it. In June 1989, under pressure from Congress, the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington cancelled the touring show, and in October 1989 Congress passed an NEA appropriations bill requiring grant recipients to pledge they would not produce "obscene" works (The Christian Science Monitor, "Chronology of a Controversy", 31 July 1990).
- The NEA appropriations bill required any grant the ICA requested to be posted on Capitol Hill for 30 days before consideration because of its role in the Mapplethorpe exhibition. In summer 1990 the National Council for the Arts turned down two of three ICA grants that peer panels had approved; the rejection was later reversed (The Daily Pennsylvanian, Peter Spiegel, "Controversy over federal arts funding hits home, again", 19 November 1990).
- ICA director Patrick Murphy said the rejection was meant as a punishment to the museum: "The feeling was that to give a grant to the Mappelthorpe museum would be an affront to Congress" (The Daily Pennsylvanian).

SOURCES
- https://www.csmonitor.com/1990/0731/l1thorpe.html
- https://www.thedp.com/article/1990/11/focus_controversy_over_federal_arts_funding_hits_home_again
